fields.Choices:
It is always 400,000 because the GIL makes each line atomic
Nothing: it can be less than 400,000 because += is a read, add and store that a thread switch can split
It is always 400,000 because ints are immutable
The program raises RuntimeError on the conflicting writes
fields.Correct: Nothing: it can be less than 400,000 because += is a read, add and store that a thread switch can split
fields.Explanation: count += 1 compiles to several bytecodes (load, add, store) and the interpreter can switch threads between them, so updates are lost. The GIL protects interpreter internals, not your read modify write sequences. Immutability of int is irrelevant: the name binding is what races. CPython never detects or raises on a data race.
fields.Hint: The GIL serialises bytecodes, not statements.
fields.Source:
Python glossary: global interpreter lock (https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-global-interpreter-lock)
Python threading documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/threading.html)

fields.Question: You must speed up a pure Python CPU bound function (no C extensions release the GIL) over 8 cores on standard CPython. Which tool gives a real speedup?
fields.Choices:
ThreadPoolExecutor with 8 workers
asyncio.gather over 8 coroutines
ProcessPoolExecutor
threading.Thread per core with a Lock around the work
fields.Correct: ProcessPoolExecutor
fields.Explanation: Separate processes each have their own interpreter and GIL, so pure Python code runs in parallel. Threads on a GIL build take turns on one core for bytecode. asyncio is single threaded cooperative concurrency and gives no CPU parallelism. Adding a Lock to threads only makes the serialisation explicit.
fields.Hint: Which option sidesteps the GIL entirely?
fields.Source:
Python concurrent.futures documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html)
Python glossary: global interpreter lock (https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-global-interpreter-lock)

fields.Question: A script downloads 500 URLs with the blocking requests library and spends almost all its time waiting on the network. Which change is the simplest one that gives a large speedup on standard CPython?
fields.Choices:
Run the downloads in a ThreadPoolExecutor
Run the downloads in a ProcessPoolExecutor with 500 processes
Wrap each requests.get in async def and gather them
Nothing helps because of the GIL
fields.Correct: Run the downloads in a ThreadPoolExecutor
fields.Explanation: Blocking socket I/O releases the GIL, so threads overlap their waits and the speedup is large. 500 processes works but costs far more memory and startup for no benefit on I/O. Wrapping a blocking call in async def still blocks the event loop, so the calls run one after another. The GIL does not block I/O concurrency.
fields.Hint: Does a thread hold the GIL while waiting on a socket?
fields.Source:
Python concurrent.futures documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html)
Python glossary: global interpreter lock (https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-global-interpreter-lock)

fields.Question:
What happens when this runs?
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with ProcessPoolExecutor() as ex:
        print(list(ex.map(lambda x: x * x, [1, 2, 3])))
fields.Choices:
It prints [1, 4, 9]
It fails because the lambda cannot be pickled to send to worker processes
It deadlocks because the pool is never shut down
It prints the results in random order
fields.Correct: It fails because the lambda cannot be pickled to send to worker processes
fields.Explanation: ProcessPoolExecutor ships the callable to worker processes with pickle, and lambdas cannot be pickled, so map raises a pickling error. Use a module level def. The with block shuts the pool down, so no deadlock. map returns results in input order regardless of completion order.
fields.Hint: How does the function reach another process?
fields.Source:
Python concurrent.futures documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html)
Python multiprocessing documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/multiprocessing.html)

fields.Question: On macOS, a script creates a multiprocessing.Pool at module top level with no if __name__ == "__main__" guard. Why does it break?
fields.Choices:
The default spawn start method re-imports the main module in each child, which tries to create the pool again
fork copies the parent's threads, causing a deadlock
Pool requires root privileges on macOS
The GIL is shared between parent and children
fields.Correct: The default spawn start method re-imports the main module in each child, which tries to create the pool again
fields.Explanation: Since Python 3.8 macOS defaults to spawn, which starts a fresh interpreter that imports the main module; unguarded top level code runs again in the child and multiprocessing raises a RuntimeError about bootstrapping. fork is not the default there and copies only the calling thread. No privileges are involved. Each process has its own GIL.
fields.Hint: What does a spawned child do with your main module?

fields.Question: A Linux service with a running logging thread calls os.fork() style multiprocessing (fork start method). The child occasionally hangs forever on its first log call. Most likely cause?
fields.Choices:
The child has no GIL
fork copied a lock that the logging thread held at fork time, and no thread exists in the child to release it
Logging handlers are disabled in child processes
The child process inherits a closed stdout
fields.Correct: fork copied a lock that the logging thread held at fork time, and no thread exists in the child to release it
fields.Explanation: fork copies memory, including locks in their held state, but only the forking thread. If another thread held the logging lock, the child's copy stays locked forever. This is why Python 3.12 warns on fork with multiple threads and 3.14 moved the Linux default to forkserver. The child does have its own GIL; handlers and stdout are inherited intact.
fields.Source:
Python multiprocessing documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/multiprocessing.html)
Python threading documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/threading.html)

fields.Question: On a free-threaded CPython 3.13t build (GIL disabled), which statement is true?
fields.Choices:
Free threading makes every list and dict operation and every += atomic
Pure Python threads can run on multiple cores at once, but unsynchronised read modify write on shared data still races
The GIL is removed from all CPython 3.13 builds by default
C extensions that are not marked as supporting free threading run without the GIL anyway
fields.Correct: Pure Python threads can run on multiple cores at once, but unsynchronised read modify write on shared data still races
fields.Explanation: The t build lets bytecode run in parallel. Built-in containers keep internal consistency with per object locks, but compound operations like += or check then set are still not atomic. The default 3.13 build still has the GIL; free threading is a separate experimental build. Importing an extension not marked free thread safe re-enables the GIL unless overridden with PYTHON_GIL=0.
fields.Hint: Parallel bytecode does not mean atomic programs.
fields.Source:
Python HOWTO: free-threaded CPython (https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html)
PEP 703: Making the Global Interpreter Lock Optional in CPython (https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/)

fields.Question: You run a free-threaded 3.13t interpreter and import a C extension that has not declared Py_mod_gil support. What does CPython do by default?
fields.Choices:
Refuses to import the module
Runs the extension without the GIL and hopes for the best
Runs that extension in a subinterpreter
Re-enables the GIL for the process and prints a warning
fields.Correct: Re-enables the GIL for the process and prints a warning
fields.Explanation: The free-threaded build re-enables the GIL at runtime when it imports an extension that has not declared it is safe, and warns, unless PYTHON_GIL=0 or -X gil=0 forces it off. It does not refuse the import, does not silently run unsafe code without the GIL by default, and does not isolate it in a subinterpreter.
fields.Hint: The default is safety over speed.

fields.Question:
Which fix makes this bank transfer correct when many threads call it on shared accounts?
def transfer(src, dst, amt):
    if balances[src] >= amt:
        balances[src] -= amt
        balances[dst] += amt
fields.Choices:
Wrap each of the three lines in its own with lock: block
Hold one lock across the balance check and both updates
Mark balances as a global
Call time.sleep(0) before the check to yield first
fields.Correct: Hold one lock across the balance check and both updates
fields.Explanation: The check and the two updates must be one atomic step, otherwise two threads can both pass the check and overdraw. Locking each line separately still lets another thread act between them. global changes scope, not synchronisation. Sleeping only changes timing and makes the race rarer, not gone.

fields.Question: A method holding a threading.Lock calls another method of the same object that also does with self.lock:. What happens?
fields.Choices:
It works, Python locks are reentrant
It raises RuntimeError: lock already held
The thread deadlocks on itself, because Lock is not reentrant
The inner with is skipped
fields.Correct: The thread deadlocks on itself, because Lock is not reentrant
fields.Explanation: threading.Lock does not track an owner, so the second acquire by the same thread blocks forever. RLock is the reentrant variant that counts acquisitions by the owning thread. Lock raises no error on a nested acquire, and with never skips its body.
fields.Hint: Which lock class counts acquisitions per owner?

fields.Question: You build a thread producer consumer with queue.Queue. How should the producer tell 4 consumer threads to stop?
fields.Choices:
Call queue.close() so consumers see an exception
Set a global flag; consumers blocked in get() will notice it
Put one sentinel value per consumer, and each consumer exits when it gets one
Call thread.stop() on each consumer
fields.Correct: Put one sentinel value per consumer, and each consumer exits when it gets one
fields.Explanation: Consumers blocked in get() only wake on an item, so a sentinel per consumer is the standard shutdown. queue.Queue only gained shutdown() in 3.13; there is no close(). A flag is not seen by a thread blocked forever in get() without a timeout. Python threads have no stop method.
fields.Hint: What wakes a thread blocked in get()?

fields.Question: A worker thread is started with daemon=True and is midway through writing a file when the main thread returns. What happens?
fields.Choices:
The interpreter waits for the daemon thread to finish
The interpreter exits without waiting, so the write can be cut off
The daemon thread is moved to a background process
Python raises an error because a thread is still running
fields.Correct: The interpreter exits without waiting, so the write can be cut off
fields.Explanation: Daemon threads are abruptly stopped at shutdown; resources like open files may not be flushed or released. Non daemon threads are the ones the interpreter joins. Threads never migrate to processes, and exiting with live daemon threads is not an error.
fields.Hint: What does the daemon flag change at exit?

fields.Question: A task submitted with executor.submit(fn) raises ValueError and nobody calls result() on the future. What does the program see?
fields.Choices:
A traceback is printed and the worker thread dies
The executor shuts down
Nothing: the exception is stored in the Future and silently ignored
The ValueError is raised in the main thread
fields.Correct: Nothing: the exception is stored in the Future and silently ignored
fields.Explanation: submit captures the exception in the Future; it is only re-raised when you call result() or inspected with exception(). The worker thread survives and keeps serving tasks. The executor is not affected and nothing is injected into the main thread, which is why unchecked futures hide bugs.

fields.Question: Explain how you choose between threads, processes and asyncio in Python for a given workload, including what free-threaded builds change.
fields.Answer:
I/O bound with blocking libraries: threads, the GIL is released during I/O. I/O bound with many connections and async libraries: asyncio, cheap tasks and explicit await points. CPU bound pure Python: processes, each has its own GIL, at the cost of pickling and memory. CPU work in NumPy or other GIL releasing C code: threads can scale.

Free-threaded 3.13t and later lets threads run bytecode in parallel, so threads become an option for CPU work, but you still need locks for compound operations and every extension must support it, otherwise the GIL comes back.
fields.Source:
Python glossary: global interpreter lock (https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-global-interpreter-lock)
Python HOWTO: free-threaded CPython (https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html)
Python concurrent.futures documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html)

fields.Question: Sketch a multithreaded web crawler in Python: fetch from a start URL, stay on one host, never fetch a URL twice, stop when done.
fields.Answer:
Shared state: a set of seen URLs guarded by a Lock, a queue.Queue of pending URLs, and a ThreadPoolExecutor or N worker threads. Each worker takes a URL, fetches it (blocking I/O releases the GIL), parses links, filters by host, and under the lock adds unseen ones to seen and to the queue. The check and add must be one critical section.

Termination: track outstanding work. Using queue.join() with task_done() after each URL works: when the counter hits zero, put sentinels to stop workers. Follow ups: per host rate limiting, retries with backoff, timeouts, and asyncio with aiohttp plus a Semaphore as the alternative.
fields.Hint: The hard parts are dedupe and knowing when you are done.
fields.Source:
Python threading documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/threading.html)
Python concurrent.futures documentation (https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html)

fields.Question:
Ten copies of handler run under asyncio.gather. Roughly how long does the whole gather take?
import asyncio, time

async def handler():
    time.sleep(1)

async def main():
    await asyncio.gather(*(handler() for _ in range(10)))
fields.Choices:
About 10 seconds, because time.sleep blocks the event loop
About 1 second, because gather runs them concurrently
About 1 second, because asyncio runs each coroutine in a thread
It raises RuntimeError for calling a blocking function
fields.Correct: About 10 seconds, because time.sleep blocks the event loop
fields.Explanation: time.sleep blocks the single event loop thread, so no other coroutine can run until it returns: the ten handlers run back to back. Using await asyncio.sleep(1) would give about 1 second. asyncio does not put coroutines in threads, and it does not detect blocking calls except as slow callback warnings in debug mode.
fields.Source:
Python Developing with asyncio (https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-dev.html)
Python asyncio Coroutines and Tasks (https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html)

fields.Question: Inside a coroutine you must call a blocking library function that takes 2 seconds and has no async version. Which call keeps the event loop responsive?
fields.Choices:
await blocking_fn()
asyncio.create_task(blocking_fn())
await asyncio.to_thread(blocking_fn)
await asyncio.sleep(0); blocking_fn()
fields.Correct: await asyncio.to_thread(blocking_fn)
fields.Explanation: to_thread runs the function in a worker thread and awaits the result, so the loop keeps serving other tasks. A plain function returns a value, not an awaitable, so await on it fails, and it would have blocked first anyway. create_task needs a coroutine, and calling blocking_fn() runs it right there. sleep(0) yields once, then the blocking call still freezes the loop.

fields.Question:
What does this print?
import asyncio

async def save():
    print("saving")

async def main():
    save()
    print("done")

asyncio.run(main())
fields.Choices:
saving then done
Only done, plus a RuntimeWarning that the coroutine was never awaited
done then saving
Nothing, it raises TypeError
fields.Correct: Only done, plus a RuntimeWarning that the coroutine was never awaited
fields.Explanation: Calling an async def function only creates a coroutine object; without await or create_task its body never runs, and Python warns when the object is garbage collected. So saving is never printed. No TypeError occurs because creating a coroutine is legal.
fields.Hint: What does calling an async function return?

fields.Question: A server fires background work with asyncio.create_task(audit(event)) and discards the return value. Occasionally an audit never completes. Why?
fields.Choices:
create_task tasks only run when awaited
Tasks created inside a handler are cancelled when the handler returns
create_task runs the coroutine in a thread pool that drops jobs under load
The event loop keeps only weak references to tasks, so an unreferenced task can be garbage collected mid flight
fields.Correct: The event loop keeps only weak references to tasks, so an unreferenced task can be garbage collected mid flight
fields.Explanation: The asyncio docs say to save a reference to the result of create_task because the loop holds only weak references; keep tasks in a set and discard on done, or use a TaskGroup. Tasks start without being awaited. They are not auto cancelled when the creator returns, and no thread pool is involved.

fields.Question: asyncio.gather(a(), b(), c()) is awaited with the default return_exceptions=False. b() raises ValueError while a() and c() are still running. What happens?
fields.Choices:
The await raises ValueError and a() and c() are cancelled
The await waits for a() and c(), then raises an ExceptionGroup
The await raises ValueError immediately, and a() and c() keep running uncancelled
The ValueError is returned in the result list
fields.Correct: The await raises ValueError immediately, and a() and c() keep running uncancelled
fields.Explanation: With return_exceptions=False the first exception propagates to the awaiter, but the other awaitables are not cancelled and continue to run, which surprises many candidates. TaskGroup is the API that cancels siblings and raises an ExceptionGroup. Returning exceptions in the list happens only with return_exceptions=True.

fields.Question: Using async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg, one child task raises KeyError. What does the async with block do?
fields.Choices:
Raises KeyError immediately and leaves the other children running
Ignores the error until all children finish, then returns their results
Cancels the remaining children, waits for them, then raises an ExceptionGroup containing the KeyError
Restarts the failed child
fields.Correct: Cancels the remaining children, waits for them, then raises an ExceptionGroup containing the KeyError
fields.Explanation: TaskGroup gives structured concurrency: on the first failure it cancels the other tasks, waits for them to finish, and raises an ExceptionGroup (catch with except*). Leaving siblings running is gather's behaviour. It never swallows errors or retries.

fields.Choices:
cancel() only takes effect while a task is sleeping in asyncio.sleep
cancel() has no effect on tasks created with create_task
The bare except catches CancelledError, which is a BaseException, so the loop just continues
queue.get() is not a cancellation point
fields.Correct: The bare except catches CancelledError, which is a BaseException, so the loop just continues
fields.Explanation: Cancellation is delivered as CancelledError at the next await. Since 3.8 it derives from BaseException, so except Exception lets it through, but a bare except catches it and the loop carries on. Catch narrower exceptions or re-raise CancelledError. Any await can be interrupted, including queue.get(), and create_task tasks are cancellable.

fields.Question: You need a single HTTP call coroutine to give up after 5 seconds in Python 3.11+. Which is correct?
fields.Choices:
fetch(timeout=5) on any coroutine
await asyncio.sleep(5) then fetch.cancel()
async with asyncio.timeout(5): await fetch()
signal.alarm(5) around the await
fields.Correct: async with asyncio.timeout(5): await fetch()
fields.Explanation: asyncio.timeout (or wait_for) cancels the inner await when the deadline passes and raises TimeoutError. Coroutines do not accept a generic timeout argument. Sleeping first delays the call by 5 seconds rather than bounding it. signal.alarm fires a signal handler, not an asyncio cancellation, and only works in the main thread.
fields.Hint: There is a context manager for deadlines.

fields.Question: An async crawler must never have more than 10 requests in flight. Which pattern enforces that?
fields.Choices:
Call asyncio.gather on batches of 10 created with create_task
Use threading.Semaphore(10) inside the coroutines
Set the event loop's max_workers to 10
Create asyncio.Semaphore(10) and wrap each fetch in async with sem:
fields.Correct: Create asyncio.Semaphore(10) and wrap each fetch in async with sem:
fields.Explanation: An asyncio.Semaphore admits at most 10 holders and suspends the rest without blocking the loop. Batches of 10 limit concurrency but stall on the slowest request in each batch, so throughput suffers, and creating tasks then gathering does not change that. threading.Semaphore would block the whole loop thread when exhausted. The event loop has no max_workers setting; that belongs to executors.
fields.Hint: Cap concurrent holders without blocking the loop.

fields.Question: An asyncio producer consumer uses queue.join() to know when all work is done, but join() never returns even though every item was processed. Most likely bug?
fields.Choices:
The queue has no maxsize
join() must be called before put()
Consumers used get_nowait() instead of get()
Consumers never call queue.task_done() after each item
fields.Correct: Consumers never call queue.task_done() after each item
fields.Explanation: join() waits until the count of unfinished tasks reaches zero; every put increments it and only task_done decrements it, so forgetting task_done leaves join blocked forever. maxsize only bounds puts. Ordering of join versus put does not matter. get_nowait versus get affects waiting, not the unfinished count.

fields.Question: Single threaded asyncio code updates a shared dict. Which version can lose updates?
fields.Choices:
value = cache[k]; await save(value); cache[k] = value + 1
cache[k] = cache[k] + 1 with no await in between
cache.setdefault(k, 0) with no await
for k in keys: cache[k] = 0 with no await in the loop
fields.Correct: value = cache[k]; await save(value); cache[k] = value + 1
fields.Explanation: Coroutines only switch at await points, so code without an await between read and write is atomic relative to other tasks. Reading, awaiting, then writing lets another task update cache[k] in the gap, and one update is lost. The other three have no suspension point between the read and the write.

fields.Question: Design a fault tolerant async work queue in Python: N workers, retries with backoff, at most M jobs in flight, clean shutdown.
fields.Answer:
Use an asyncio.Queue with maxsize for backpressure and a TaskGroup of N workers. Each worker loops on await queue.get(), runs the job under asyncio.timeout, and on failure re-enqueues with an attempt count and exponential backoff with jitter, up to a limit, then sends it to a dead letter list. Always call task_done in a finally block.

Shutdown: await queue.join(), then cancel workers (or use Queue.shutdown in 3.13). Never swallow CancelledError. Blocking calls go through to_thread. Mention idempotency, since retries mean a job can run twice, and persisting the queue if jobs must survive a crash.
fields.Source:
Python asyncio Queues (https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-queue.html)
Python asyncio Coroutines and Tasks (https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html)

fields.Choices:
Yes: volatile makes every operation on the field atomic
Yes: int writes are always atomic in Java
No: volatile fields cannot be modified by more than one thread
No: volatile gives visibility, but count++ is still a separate read and write that can interleave
fields.Correct: No: volatile gives visibility, but count++ is still a separate read and write that can interleave
fields.Explanation: volatile guarantees each read sees the latest write and orders memory, but ++ is read, add, write, and two threads can read the same value and lose an increment. Use AtomicInteger or LongAdder or synchronized. Single int writes being atomic does not make the compound operation atomic. Many threads can write a volatile field.
fields.Source:
Java Language Specification, Chapter 17 Threads and Locks (https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-17.html)
Java AtomicInteger API (https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/atomic/AtomicInteger.html)

fields.Choices:
Make running a static field
Call Thread.yield() inside the loop
Wrap the assignment in stop() in a try block
Declare running as volatile
fields.Correct: Declare running as volatile
fields.Explanation: Without a happens before edge, the JIT may hoist the read of running out of the loop and the worker never sees the write. volatile creates that edge for every read. static changes ownership, not visibility. Thread.yield gives no memory guarantee. A try block has no memory semantics.
fields.Hint: The JIT can hoist a non volatile read.
fields.Source: Java Language Specification, Chapter 17 Threads and Locks (https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-17.html)

fields.Choices:
Without volatile on instance, another thread can see a non null reference to a partly constructed object; declare it volatile
synchronized does not work on static methods; use a ReentrantLock
The second null check is redundant; remove it
It creates two instances under contention; make the constructor private
fields.Correct: Without volatile on instance, another thread can see a non null reference to a partly constructed object; declare it volatile
fields.Explanation: The write of the reference can become visible before the constructor's field writes, so a thread skipping the lock may use an object with default field values. volatile forbids that reordering for the publication. synchronized works fine on class locks. The second check is what prevents two instances. A private constructor does nothing for thread safety.
fields.Hint: What can a thread that skips the lock observe?
fields.Source:
The Double-Checked Locking is Broken Declaration (https://www.cs.umd.edu/~pugh/java/memoryModel/DoubleCheckedLocking.html)
Java Language Specification, Chapter 17 Threads and Locks (https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-17.html)

fields.Question: Which lazy singleton is thread safe without any explicit locking or volatile?
fields.Choices:
A private static nested Holder class with a static final INSTANCE field
A static field assigned in getInstance() on first call
A non volatile field checked with double checked locking
An instance field initialised in a constructor of the outer class
fields.Correct: A private static nested Holder class with a static final INSTANCE field
fields.Explanation: Class initialisation is guaranteed by the JVM to run once, under a lock, and to happen before any use of the class, so the holder idiom is lazy and safe. Plain lazy assignment races. Double checked locking without volatile is unsafe. An instance field gives one value per object, not a singleton.
fields.Source: Java Language Specification, Chapter 17 Threads and Locks (https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-17.html)

fields.Question: An object with only final fields set in its constructor is published to another thread through a plain non volatile field, and this does not escape during construction. What does the JMM guarantee to the reader that sees the reference?
fields.Choices:
Nothing, it may see default values in the final fields
It sees the final fields only if the reader uses synchronized
It sees all fields, including non final ones, fully initialised
It sees the correctly constructed values of the final fields
fields.Correct: It sees the correctly constructed values of the final fields
fields.Explanation: JLS 17.5 guarantees that a thread seeing a reference to an object after its constructor finished sees the final fields' constructed values, even through a data race. That guarantee does not extend to non final fields. No reader side synchronisation is needed for the final fields.
fields.Source: Java Language Specification, Chapter 17 Threads and Locks (https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-17.html)

fields.Question: Thread T writes x = 42 and exits. The main thread calls t.join() and then reads x (a plain field). What does it read?
fields.Choices:
Possibly 0, because x is not volatile
42 only if x is final
Possibly 0, because join() only waits and has no memory effect
42, because everything T did happens before join() returns
fields.Correct: 42, because everything T did happens before join() returns
fields.Explanation: JLS 17.4.5 defines that all actions in a thread happen before another thread successfully returns from join on it, so the write is visible. volatile and final are not needed here. join is a synchronisation action with memory effects, not just a wait.
fields.Hint: join is a happens before edge.
fields.Source: Java Language Specification, Chapter 17 Threads and Locks (https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-17.html)

fields.Question: Two threads write different values to a plain non volatile long field on a 32 bit JVM. What can a reader observe according to the JLS?
fields.Choices:
Only one of the two written values
A torn value: the high 32 bits of one write and the low 32 bits of the other
Only the value written last in wall clock time
An exception from the JVM
fields.Correct: A torn value: the high 32 bits of one write and the low 32 bits of the other
fields.Explanation: JLS 17.7 allows non volatile long and double writes to be split into two 32 bit writes, so mixed halves are legal. Declaring the field volatile makes them atomic. Most 64 bit JVMs do not tear in practice, but the spec permits it. There is no notion of last in wall clock time without ordering, and the JVM does not throw.
fields.Source: Java Language Specification, Chapter 17 Threads and Locks (https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-17.html)

fields.Question: A getter reads a field without synchronisation while the setter writes it inside synchronized(this). Is the reader guaranteed to see the latest value?
fields.Choices:
Yes: synchronized on the writer flushes the value to all threads
Yes: reads of references are atomic
No, and the read can also throw ConcurrentModificationException
No: happens before needs both sides to synchronise on the same monitor
fields.Correct: No: happens before needs both sides to synchronise on the same monitor
fields.Explanation: An unlock happens before a later lock of the same monitor. A reader that never locks gets no edge and may read a stale value. The idea of flushing to main memory on write alone is a common but wrong mental model. Atomicity of reference reads is not visibility. ConcurrentModificationException is a collection iterator check, unrelated.
fields.Hint: Both sides need the same lock.
fields.Source: Java Language Specification, Chapter 17 Threads and Locks (https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-17.html)

fields.Question: Which consumer code correctly waits for a condition with wait() and notifyAll()?
fields.Correct: synchronized (lock) { while (!ready) lock.wait(); }
fields.Explanation: wait must be called while holding the monitor and inside a loop, because of spurious wakeups and because another thread may change the condition before the woken thread reacquires the lock. An if checks only once. Calling wait without owning the monitor throws IllegalMonitorStateException. Waiting first misses a notification that already happened.
fields.Source: Java Language Specification, Chapter 17 Threads and Locks (https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-17.html)

fields.Question: Several threads call put on a shared java.util.HashMap without locking. Which outcome is possible?
fields.Choices:
Nothing bad, because put is synchronized internally
A guaranteed ConcurrentModificationException on the second put
Lost entries and a corrupted internal table
A compile time error
fields.Correct: Lost entries and a corrupted internal table
fields.Explanation: HashMap is not thread safe; concurrent resizes can drop entries or corrupt buckets (older JDKs could even form cycles and spin). Its methods are not synchronized. ConcurrentModificationException comes from iterators detecting modification, and it is best effort, not guaranteed. The compiler has no idea about thread usage.

fields.Question: Which of these is NOT a safe publication of a mutable object to other threads?
fields.Choices:
Storing it in a ConcurrentHashMap that readers get from
Assigning it to a plain non final, non volatile field that readers poll
Assigning it to a volatile field
Initialising it in a static initialiser
fields.Correct: Assigning it to a plain non final, non volatile field that readers poll
fields.Explanation: Safe publication needs a happens before edge: static initialisers, volatile fields, final fields, locks and concurrent collections all provide one. A plain field does not, so readers may see the reference before the object's state. That is why the other three are standard safe idioms.
fields.Hint: Which one creates no happens before edge?
fields.Source:
Java Language Specification, Chapter 17 Threads and Locks (https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-17.html)
Java ConcurrentHashMap API (https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/ConcurrentHashMap.html)

fields.Question: Explain happens before in the Java Memory Model and name the edges you would rely on in interview code.
fields.Answer:
If action A happens before B, B sees A's effects and they are not reordered across each other. Without that edge, a data race exists and reads may be stale or reordered.

Edges: program order within a thread; unlock then later lock of the same monitor; volatile write then a later read of the same field; Thread.start before the started thread's actions; a thread's actions before join returns; final field freeze at the end of a constructor; and the java.util.concurrent guarantees, such as putting into a concurrent queue before taking out. Transitivity chains them.
fields.Source: Java Language Specification, Chapter 17 Threads and Locks (https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se21/html/jls-17.html)

fields.Choices:
Nothing: ConcurrentHashMap makes the whole method atomic
It throws ConcurrentModificationException
The get and put are separate operations, so concurrent increments are lost; use counts.merge(k, 1, Integer::sum)
get returns a copy, so the put has no effect
fields.Correct: The get and put are separate operations, so concurrent increments are lost; use counts.merge(k, 1, Integer::sum)
fields.Explanation: Each call is thread safe on its own, but two threads can read the same old value and both write old plus one. merge, compute or computeIfAbsent perform the read modify write atomically per key. ConcurrentHashMap never throws ConcurrentModificationException. get returns the stored reference, not a copy.
fields.Hint: Individual calls are atomic. Sequences are not.

fields.Question: What does ConcurrentHashMap.put("a", null) do?
fields.Choices:
Stores a null value like HashMap does
Removes the key a
Is ignored silently
Throws NullPointerException
fields.Correct: Throws NullPointerException
fields.Explanation: ConcurrentHashMap rejects null keys and values because a null from get could not distinguish absent from mapped to null without a race. HashMap allows them. put never removes keys, and nothing is silently ignored.
fields.Hint: Why would null be ambiguous under concurrency?

fields.Question: Inside counts.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> loadFromDatabase(k)) the loader takes 2 seconds. What is the main risk?
fields.Choices:
The loader may run several times for the same key
The value is not visible to other threads after it returns
computeIfAbsent cannot be used with lambdas
Other updates on keys in the same bin block for the duration, since the function runs while holding a lock
fields.Correct: Other updates on keys in the same bin block for the duration, since the function runs while holding a lock
fields.Explanation: The docs say the function is applied at most once per call and other updates may block while it runs, so keep it short and never touch the map recursively from inside it. Running multiple times is the putIfAbsent pattern's problem. The result is safely published. Lambdas are the normal argument.

fields.Question: Threads are adding to a ConcurrentHashMap. What does size() return during the updates?
fields.Choices:
An exact count, locking the whole map
An estimate that may not reflect in flight updates
Always the size at the time the map was created
It throws if a resize is in progress
fields.Correct: An estimate that may not reflect in flight updates
fields.Explanation: Aggregate status methods like size and isEmpty are only useful when the map is not being concurrently updated; they may reflect transient states. There is no global lock in ConcurrentHashMap. It never throws because of resizing.

fields.Question: One thread iterates a ConcurrentHashMap's entrySet while another thread adds and removes keys. What happens?
fields.Choices:
Iteration completes without exception and may or may not reflect the changes
ConcurrentModificationException is thrown
The iterating thread blocks until writers finish
The iterator sees a full snapshot taken when it was created
fields.Correct: Iteration completes without exception and may or may not reflect the changes
fields.Explanation: ConcurrentHashMap iterators are weakly consistent: they never throw ConcurrentModificationException, they reflect the state at some point at or since creation, and may show later changes. They do not block writers or take a snapshot copy. Snapshots are CopyOnWriteArrayList's behaviour.

fields.Question: A hot metrics counter is incremented by 64 threads and read once a minute. Which choice has the best throughput?
fields.Choices:
AtomicLong
A volatile long with ++
A long guarded by synchronized
LongAdder
fields.Correct: LongAdder
fields.Explanation: LongAdder spreads updates over striped cells, so contended increments rarely collide, and sum() is cheap enough for occasional reads. AtomicLong is correct but all threads CAS one memory location and retry under contention. volatile ++ is not atomic. synchronized is correct but serialises every increment.
fields.Hint: Contention on one word is the bottleneck.
fields.Source:
Java LongAdder API (https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/atomic/LongAdder.html)
Java AtomicInteger API (https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/atomic/AtomicInteger.html)

fields.Question: You need to keep the maximum value seen across threads in an AtomicLong. Which is correct?
fields.Correct: max.accumulateAndGet(v, Math::max)
fields.Explanation: accumulateAndGet runs a CAS loop so the read and update are atomic. The if and set version checks then acts, so a larger value from another thread can be overwritten by a smaller one. set(Math.max(get, v)) has the same race. getAndAdd changes the value temporarily and other threads observe garbage.
fields.Hint: Check then act on an atomic is still a race.

fields.Choices:
If process throws, unlock is skipped and the lock is held forever
lock() must be inside the try block for it to work at all
ReentrantLock cannot be used in methods that throw
Nothing, this is the recommended form
fields.Correct: If process throws, unlock is skipped and the lock is held forever
fields.Explanation: Unlock must be in finally so it runs on exceptions. The recommended form is lock() immediately before try and unlock() in finally; putting lock inside try risks unlocking a lock you never acquired. Throwing methods are fine with locks. As written it is a leak.
fields.Hint: What runs on every exit path?

fields.Question: Which capability does ReentrantLock offer that a synchronized block does not?
fields.Choices:
tryLock with a timeout, so a thread can give up instead of waiting forever
Reentrancy for the owning thread
Automatic release when the block exits
Mutual exclusion and visibility between threads
fields.Correct: tryLock with a timeout, so a thread can give up instead of waiting forever
fields.Explanation: tryLock(timeout), lockInterruptibly, fairness and multiple Condition objects are ReentrantLock features. Both are reentrant and both give mutual exclusion and happens before. Automatic release is the advantage of synchronized, not ReentrantLock.

fields.Question: Which workload suits CopyOnWriteArrayList?
fields.Choices:
A queue with constant appends from many producers
A large buffer updated on every request
A counter list incremented in place by many threads
A listener list read and iterated constantly but modified rarely
fields.Correct: A listener list read and iterated constantly but modified rarely
fields.Explanation: Every mutation copies the whole array, so reads and iteration are lock free and snapshot based, which suits read mostly lists like listeners. Frequent appends or updates copy repeatedly and become very slow. In place element increments are not atomic anyway.

fields.Question: A service uses Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16) and producers submit faster than tasks finish for an hour. What eventually happens?
fields.Choices:
New submissions are rejected with RejectedExecutionException once 16 tasks are running
The pool adds threads beyond 16 to catch up
Heap grows until OutOfMemoryError, because the pool's LinkedBlockingQueue is unbounded
submit blocks the producer until a thread is free
fields.Correct: Heap grows until OutOfMemoryError, because the pool's LinkedBlockingQueue is unbounded
fields.Explanation: newFixedThreadPool uses an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue, so tasks pile up without limit. Rejection only happens with a bounded queue or after shutdown. Threads beyond core are created only when the queue refuses an offer, which an unbounded queue never does. submit never blocks in ThreadPoolExecutor.
fields.Hint: Look at the queue the factory method uses.
fields.Source:
Java Executors API (https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/Executors.html)
Java ThreadPoolExecutor API (https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/ThreadPoolExecutor.html)

fields.Question: A ThreadPoolExecutor has core 4, max 16 and an ArrayBlockingQueue of 100. 4 tasks are running, the queue is empty, and a new task arrives. What does the executor do?
fields.Choices:
Starts a 5th thread immediately
Rejects the task
Puts the task in the queue; it only creates threads beyond 4 once the queue is full
Runs the task in the caller thread
fields.Correct: Puts the task in the queue; it only creates threads beyond 4 once the queue is full
fields.Explanation: The order is: below core size create a thread, otherwise try to queue, and only if the queue is full create threads up to max, then reject. Many expect threads to grow first. Rejection and caller runs only apply once both queue and max are exhausted.

fields.Question: You want a bounded ThreadPoolExecutor to slow producers down instead of failing when saturated. Which rejection policy does that?
fields.Choices:
CallerRunsPolicy
AbortPolicy
DiscardPolicy
DiscardOldestPolicy
fields.Correct: CallerRunsPolicy
fields.Explanation: CallerRunsPolicy runs the rejected task in the submitting thread, which throttles the producer naturally. AbortPolicy is the default and throws RejectedExecutionException. DiscardPolicy silently drops the task and DiscardOldestPolicy drops the oldest queued one; both lose work.
fields.Hint: Push the work back onto the producer.

fields.Question: A Runnable throws an unchecked exception. With executor.submit(r) nobody calls get(). With executor.execute(r) the same happens. Which is true?
fields.Choices:
Both print the stack trace
submit hides it in the Future; execute lets it reach the thread's uncaught exception handler, so it is printed by default
Both swallow the exception silently
submit prints it and execute swallows it
fields.Correct: submit hides it in the Future; execute lets it reach the thread's uncaught exception handler, so it is printed by default
fields.Explanation: submit wraps the task in a FutureTask that catches the exception and stores it for get(). execute runs the Runnable directly, so the exception propagates to the worker's UncaughtExceptionHandler, which prints it, and the worker is replaced. That is why unchecked submit futures lose errors.
fields.Hint: Where does a FutureTask put an exception?

fields.Question: Which sequence shuts down an executor gracefully, then forcefully if tasks hang?
fields.Choices:
shutdownNow() then shutdown()
awaitTermination(timeout) without calling shutdown()
close the JVM with System.exit()
shutdown(), then awaitTermination(timeout), then shutdownNow() if it returned false
fields.Correct: shutdown(), then awaitTermination(timeout), then shutdownNow() if it returned false
fields.Explanation: shutdown stops accepting tasks and lets queued ones finish, awaitTermination waits with a bound, and shutdownNow interrupts running tasks and returns the unstarted ones. shutdownNow first discards queued work. awaitTermination without shutdown just waits out the timeout because the pool never terminates. System.exit is not graceful.

fields.Question: f is a CompletableFuture that has already completed. On which thread does the function passed to f.thenApply(fn) run?
fields.Choices:
Always a ForkJoinPool.commonPool() thread
The thread that originally completed f
The thread that calls thenApply
A new thread created for the callback
fields.Correct: The thread that calls thenApply
fields.Explanation: Non async stages run on the thread that completes the previous stage, or, if it is already complete, on the thread registering the callback. Since f is done, the caller runs fn. Only the Async variants without an executor use the common pool. No thread is created per callback.

fields.Question: A web app on a 16 core server runs blocking JDBC calls in CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> query()) without an executor. Under load latency explodes. Why?
fields.Choices:
supplyAsync creates a new thread per call and the OS runs out
JDBC drivers forbid use from CompletableFuture
supplyAsync runs the query on the caller thread
supplyAsync uses ForkJoinPool.commonPool, sized to cores minus one, which blocking calls exhaust
fields.Correct: supplyAsync uses ForkJoinPool.commonPool, sized to cores minus one, which blocking calls exhaust
fields.Explanation: Without an executor the async methods use the common pool, which has about cores minus one threads shared by the whole JVM, including parallel streams. Blocking I/O there starves everything. Pass a dedicated executor sized for the blocking work. It does not create a thread per task and does not run on the caller.

fields.Question: supplyAsync(() -> fetch()).thenApply(this::parse).exceptionally(ex -> fallback()). fetch throws. What happens?
fields.Choices:
parse runs with null and then exceptionally is called
The exception is thrown on the thread that created the chain
exceptionally receives the raw exception and parse runs afterwards
parse is skipped and exceptionally receives a CompletionException wrapping the original
fields.Correct: parse is skipped and exceptionally receives a CompletionException wrapping the original
fields.Explanation: An exception completes the stage exceptionally and dependent stages like thenApply are skipped, so the failure propagates to exceptionally, usually wrapped in CompletionException; unwrap with getCause. parse never sees null. Exceptions are not rethrown to the building thread unless it calls join or get.

fields.Question: On JDK 21, many virtual threads block on network I/O inside synchronized blocks and throughput collapses to the carrier count. What is the cause and the JDK 21 fix?
fields.Choices:
Blocking inside synchronized pins the virtual thread to its carrier; replace with ReentrantLock (JDK 24 removed this pinning)
Virtual threads cannot do network I/O; use platform threads
The virtual thread pool is too small; raise it with Executors.newFixedThreadPool
synchronized is disallowed on virtual threads and throws
fields.Correct: Blocking inside synchronized pins the virtual thread to its carrier; replace with ReentrantLock (JDK 24 removed this pinning)
fields.Explanation: In JDK 21 a virtual thread that blocks while holding a monitor cannot unmount, so it occupies the carrier thread. ReentrantLock does not pin. JEP 491 in JDK 24 lets virtual threads unmount inside synchronized. Virtual threads are made for blocking I/O. They should not be pooled, and synchronized is legal.
fields.Hint: What stops a virtual thread unmounting?
fields.Source:
JEP 444: Virtual Threads (https://openjdk.org/jeps/444)
JEP 491: Synchronize Virtual Threads without Pinning (https://openjdk.org/jeps/491)

fields.Question: Which workload gains nothing from switching to virtual threads?
fields.Choices:
A CPU bound image resizer that keeps every core busy
A server handling 50,000 mostly idle HTTP requests
A fan out of 200 blocking REST calls per request
A thread per connection chat server
fields.Correct: A CPU bound image resizer that keeps every core busy
fields.Explanation: Virtual threads make blocking cheap so you can have millions of waiting tasks; they do not add CPU. A CPU bound workload is limited by cores whatever the thread type. The other three spend most time blocked and are the intended use. JEP 444 also says not to pool virtual threads; use a Semaphore to limit concurrency.
fields.Hint: Virtual threads are not faster threads.

fields.Choices:
It prints 1
It prints 0
fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!
It panics with send on closed channel
fields.Correct: fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!
fields.Explanation: An unbuffered send blocks until a receiver is ready. main is the only goroutine and it is blocked in the send, so the runtime detects that every goroutine is blocked and aborts. It never reaches the print. Nothing closed the channel.

fields.Choices:
It deadlocks
It prints 0
It prints 1
It does not compile
fields.Correct: It prints 1
fields.Explanation: A buffered channel with free capacity accepts the send without a receiver, so the value is stored and the receive returns it. Deadlock happens only when the buffer is full or zero sized. 0 would be the result of receiving from a closed empty channel.

fields.Question:
What does this print?
ch := make(chan int, 1)
ch <- 5
close(ch)
v, ok := <-ch
fmt.Println(v, ok)
v, ok = <-ch
fmt.Println(v, ok)
fields.Choices:
5 true then 0 false
5 true then a panic
5 true then the program blocks forever
5 false then 0 false
fields.Correct: 5 true then 0 false
fields.Explanation: Receiving from a closed channel first drains buffered values with ok true, then returns the zero value with ok false immediately. Only sending on a closed channel panics. Receives on closed channels never block.
fields.Hint: Closed channels drain, then yield zero values.

fields.Question: Which operation panics?
fields.Choices:
Receiving from a closed channel
Receiving from a nil channel
Sending on a nil channel
Sending on a closed channel
fields.Correct: Sending on a closed channel
fields.Explanation: A send on a closed channel panics, as do closing a closed or nil channel. Receiving from a closed channel returns the zero value. Sending or receiving on a nil channel blocks forever, it does not panic.
fields.Hint: One of these blocks rather than panics.

fields.Question: Three producer goroutines send results on one channel that a single consumer ranges over. Who should close the channel?
fields.Choices:
Each producer, when it finishes
A separate goroutine that waits on a WaitGroup for all producers, then closes it
The consumer, after it reads enough values
Nobody, channels must never be closed
fields.Correct: A separate goroutine that waits on a WaitGroup for all producers, then closes it
fields.Explanation: Closing signals no more values and only the sender side can know that; with many senders, coordinate with a WaitGroup and close once. If each producer closes, the second close or a later send panics. The receiver closing races with sends that then panic. Leaving it open makes range never end.
fields.Hint: close is a sender decision, done once.
fields.Source:
Effective Go: Concurrency (https://go.dev/doc/effective_go#concurrency)
Go sync package (https://pkg.go.dev/sync)

fields.Question: In a select merging two input channels, you set a variable to nil after that channel is closed. Why does that work?
fields.Choices:
A nil channel's case is never ready, so select stops choosing it
A nil channel returns zero values instantly so select drains it
Setting it to nil closes the channel a second time safely
It makes select panic, which the loop recovers from
fields.Correct: A nil channel's case is never ready, so select stops choosing it
fields.Explanation: Operations on nil channels block forever, so in a select their cases are effectively disabled; once both are nil you exit. A closed channel, by contrast, is always ready and would spin returning zero values. Assigning nil does not close anything, and no panic is involved.
fields.Hint: Closed is always ready, nil is never ready.

fields.Question: Both cases of a select are ready on every iteration. Which case runs?
fields.Choices:
Always the first case in source order
Always the case whose channel has more buffered items
One is chosen uniformly at random
Both run, in source order
fields.Correct: One is chosen uniformly at random
fields.Explanation: The spec says if multiple cases can proceed, a single one is chosen via uniform pseudo random selection. There is no priority by source order or buffer length, and exactly one case executes per select. To prioritise, use nested selects.
fields.Hint: There is no priority in select.

fields.Question: What does a default case in select do?
fields.Choices:
Runs after a one second timeout
Runs only if all channels are closed
Runs after every other case completes
Runs immediately when no other case is ready, making the select non blocking
fields.Correct: Runs immediately when no other case is ready, making the select non blocking
fields.Explanation: With default, select never blocks: if nothing is ready it takes default. A timeout needs a time.After or timer case. Closed channels are ready, so their cases run, not default. Only one case runs per select.

fields.Question: A long running HTTP server has a handler goroutine stuck forever on a receive that no one will send. Does the runtime report deadlock?
fields.Choices:
Yes: the runtime panics in that goroutine
Yes: the server crashes with all goroutines are asleep
No, but the goroutine is garbage collected after a minute
No: deadlock is only detected when every goroutine is blocked, so the stuck goroutine just leaks
fields.Correct: No: deadlock is only detected when every goroutine is blocked, so the stuck goroutine just leaks
fields.Explanation: The runtime check only fires when no goroutine can make progress at all. Servers always have runnable or network waiting goroutines, so individual stuck goroutines leak silently with their stacks. Goroutines are never garbage collected while blocked. Find them with pprof goroutine profiles or goleak.
fields.Hint: Detection is global, not per goroutine.
fields.Source:
The Go Programming Language Specification (https://go.dev/ref/spec)
Go context package (https://pkg.go.dev/context)

fields.Question: for v := range ch { ... } in the consumer never ends even though the producer finished sending. What is missing?
fields.Choices:
The consumer should use a buffered channel
range needs a select around it
The channel must be nil to end the loop
The producer never called close(ch)
fields.Correct: The producer never called close(ch)
fields.Explanation: range over a channel receives until the channel is closed and drained. Without close it waits forever for another value. Buffering changes nothing about termination. select is not required. A nil channel would block forever, not end the loop.
fields.Hint: How does range know there are no more values?

fields.Question: Which idiom limits a loop to at most 5 goroutines running a task at once?
fields.Choices:
An unbuffered channel that every goroutine receives from
runtime.GOMAXPROCS(5)
A buffered channel of capacity 5: send before starting work, receive when done
sync.WaitGroup with Add(5)
fields.Correct: A buffered channel of capacity 5: send before starting work, receive when done
fields.Explanation: A buffered channel acts as a counting semaphore: the 6th send blocks until someone receives. An unbuffered channel used that way blocks every goroutine until a sender appears. GOMAXPROCS limits OS threads running Go code, not goroutines. A WaitGroup counts completion and does not limit concurrency. x/sync/semaphore and errgroup.SetLimit are library alternatives.
fields.Source:
Effective Go: Concurrency (https://go.dev/doc/effective_go#concurrency)
Go errgroup package (https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/sync/errgroup)

fields.Question: Write the shape of a Go worker pool pipeline: read jobs, N workers process them, collect results, and stop everything on the first error or a cancelled request.
fields.Answer:
Use errgroup.WithContext(ctx). One goroutine sends jobs on a jobs channel and closes it when done, selecting on ctx.Done() for every send. N workers range over jobs and send results, also selecting on ctx.Done(). A worker returns its error, which cancels ctx for all. Close the results channel after g.Wait() in a separate goroutine, and the caller ranges over results.

Talking points: only senders close channels, every blocking send has a cancel path to avoid leaks, bound concurrency with N or SetLimit, and run with -race.
fields.Source:
Go errgroup package (https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/sync/errgroup)
Go context package (https://pkg.go.dev/context)

fields.Choices:
The query goroutine, which blocks forever on the unbuffered send because no one receives
Nothing, the goroutine exits when the function returns
The timer created by time.After, permanently
The channel, which must be closed explicitly to be freed
fields.Correct: The query goroutine, which blocks forever on the unbuffered send because no one receives
fields.Explanation: After the timeout no one will ever receive from ch, so the goroutine blocks on ch <- forever and leaks with its stack. Make ch buffered with capacity 1 so the send always completes. Goroutines are not killed when their creator returns. Since Go 1.23 an unreferenced time.After timer is collectable. Channels do not need closing to be garbage collected.
fields.Hint: Who receives after the timeout fires?
fields.Source:
Go 1.23 Release Notes (https://go.dev/doc/go1.23)
The Go Programming Language Specification (https://go.dev/ref/spec)

fields.Question: Why does go vet complain about ctx, _ := context.WithTimeout(parent, d)?
fields.Choices:
WithTimeout returns an error that must be checked
Discarding cancel leaks the context's resources until the timeout fires; call defer cancel()
The parent context must be context.Background()
Timeouts must be set with time.Sleep instead
fields.Correct: Discarding cancel leaks the context's resources until the timeout fires; call defer cancel()
fields.Explanation: The lostcancel check flags it because the child context and its timer stay registered with the parent until cancel is called or the deadline passes. The second result is a CancelFunc, not an error. Any parent works. time.Sleep is not a cancellation mechanism.
fields.Hint: What is the second return value?

fields.Question: A worker loop does heavy work in iterations. How does it stop promptly when its context is cancelled?
fields.Choices:
Nothing is needed, cancel() kills goroutines that hold the context
Check ctx.Done() or ctx.Err() each iteration and return
Call runtime.Goexit from the parent
Recover from the panic that cancel() raises
fields.Correct: Check ctx.Done() or ctx.Err() each iteration and return
fields.Explanation: Cancellation in Go is cooperative: cancel closes the Done channel and code must observe it. Nothing forcibly stops a goroutine. Goexit only ends the calling goroutine. Cancelling a context never panics.

fields.Question: Two goroutines write to the same plain map without locking. What happens?
fields.Choices:
The writes are serialised internally and both succeed
A recoverable panic is raised
It is safe because each goroutine writes different keys
The runtime can abort with fatal error: concurrent map writes, which recover cannot catch
fields.Correct: The runtime can abort with fatal error: concurrent map writes, which recover cannot catch
fields.Explanation: Go maps are not safe for concurrent writes; the runtime detects some cases and throws a fatal error that kills the process and cannot be recovered. There is no internal locking. Different keys do not help because writes can trigger growth of shared buckets. Use sync.Mutex, sync.RWMutex or sync.Map.
fields.Source:
Go FAQ: Why are map operations not defined to be atomic? (https://go.dev/doc/faq#atomic_maps)
Go Data Race Detector (https://go.dev/doc/articles/race_detector)

fields.Choices:
wg.Done() should be called before the work
WaitGroup must be passed by value
wg.Add(1) runs inside the goroutine, so Wait can run before any Add
Wait only waits for the first goroutine
fields.Correct: wg.Add(1) runs inside the goroutine, so Wait can run before any Add
fields.Explanation: Add must happen before the goroutine starts, in the parent, otherwise Wait may see a zero counter and return immediately. Done goes after the work, usually deferred. Passing a WaitGroup by value copies it so Done affects a copy; pass a pointer. Wait waits for the counter to reach zero.

fields.Choices:
3, 3 and 3
Undefined values because i is shared
0, 1 and 2
It does not compile
fields.Correct: 0, 1 and 2
fields.Explanation: Since Go 1.22 each loop iteration has its own i, so each closure captures a distinct variable and prints 0, 1 and 2 in some order. Before 1.22 the single shared i was usually 3 by the time goroutines ran, and that was a data race. It compiles fine.

fields.Question: A Counter struct has a sync.Mutex field and a method with a value receiver: func (c Counter) Inc() { c.mu.Lock(); c.n++; c.mu.Unlock() }. What is wrong?
fields.Choices:
The value receiver copies the struct and its mutex, so the lock protects nothing and the increment is lost
sync.Mutex must be a pointer field
Lock and Unlock must be deferred
Nothing, it is correct
fields.Correct: The value receiver copies the struct and its mutex, so the lock protects nothing and the increment is lost
fields.Explanation: Each call locks a fresh copy of the mutex and increments a copy of n, so the original never changes and go vet's copylocks check warns. Use a pointer receiver. A mutex value field is the normal style. Deferring is optional here.
fields.Hint: What does a value receiver receive?

fields.Question: A method holding mu.Lock() calls another method that also calls mu.Lock() on the same sync.Mutex. What happens?
fields.Choices:
The goroutine deadlocks, because Go mutexes are not reentrant
It succeeds, the mutex counts nested locks
It panics with recursive lock
The second Lock is ignored
fields.Correct: The goroutine deadlocks, because Go mutexes are not reentrant
fields.Explanation: sync.Mutex has no owner, so the second Lock waits for an Unlock that can never come. Go deliberately has no reentrant mutex; split into locked and unlocked internal methods. It does not panic or ignore the call.

fields.Question: Several goroutines need a lazily built config, built exactly once. Which is the idiomatic choice?
fields.Choices:
sync.Once with once.Do(load)
if cfg == nil { cfg = load() } in each goroutine
A buffered channel of size 1 holding the config
An atomic bool checked before load
fields.Correct: sync.Once with once.Do(load)
fields.Explanation: once.Do runs load exactly once and every caller returns only after it has completed, with happens before. The nil check races and can build twice. A channel can work but is clumsy and a receive takes the value. An atomic flag checked before loading lets callers proceed before the load finishes or load twice. Go 1.21 also added sync.OnceValue.
fields.Hint: There is a primitive for this.
fields.Source:
Go sync package (https://pkg.go.dev/sync)
The Go Memory Model (https://go.dev/ref/mem)

fields.Question: A goroutine holds mu.RLock() and, through a helper, calls mu.RLock() again while a writer is waiting in mu.Lock(). What can happen?
fields.Choices:
Nothing, read locks are always shareable
A panic for recursive read locking
Deadlock: the waiting writer blocks new readers, including the second RLock
The writer is starved forever
fields.Correct: Deadlock: the waiting writer blocks new readers, including the second RLock
fields.Explanation: The sync docs prohibit recursive read locking: once a writer calls Lock, new RLock calls block until the writer finishes, and the writer waits for the first read lock, so they deadlock. Read locks are shareable only while no writer waits. There is no panic. Go's RWMutex prevents writer starvation by design.
fields.Hint: A pending writer blocks new readers.

fields.Question: go test -race passes on your code. What does that prove?
fields.Choices:
That the code is free of data races
That the code cannot deadlock
Nothing, -race only checks for goroutine leaks
Only that no races happened on the paths the tests executed
fields.Correct: Only that no races happened on the paths the tests executed
fields.Explanation: The race detector instruments memory accesses at runtime and only finds races that actually occur during the run, so untested paths may still race. It has no false positives but can miss races. It does not detect deadlocks or leaks.

fields.Question: What is a goroutine leak, what causes it, and how do you find and prevent one?
fields.Answer:
A goroutine that blocks forever, so its stack and everything it references are never freed. Causes: a send or receive no one will complete (abandoned result channel after a timeout), ranging over a channel nobody closes, waiting on a mutex or WaitGroup that is never released, and loops that ignore ctx.Done().

Find: runtime.NumGoroutine trending up, pprof goroutine profiles grouped by stack, and go.uber.org/goleak in tests. Prevent: every blocking operation has a cancel path through select on ctx.Done(), buffer result channels of abandoned workers, document who closes each channel, and tie goroutine lifetimes to errgroup or WaitGroup.
fields.Source:
Go context package (https://pkg.go.dev/context)
Go sync package (https://pkg.go.dev/sync)

fields.Question:
This token bucket allow() is called from many threads. Which statement is right?
def allow(self):
    now = time.monotonic()
    self.tokens = min(self.cap, self.tokens + (now - self.last) * self.rate)
    self.last = now
    if self.tokens >= 1:
        self.tokens -= 1
        return True
    return False
fields.Choices:
It is safe because the GIL makes the method atomic
It races: two threads can both see tokens >= 1 and both decrement, so the fix is one lock around refill, check and decrement
It is safe because time.monotonic() is thread safe
It races only in the refill line, so locking that line alone fixes it
fields.Correct: It races: two threads can both see tokens >= 1 and both decrement, so the fix is one lock around refill, check and decrement
fields.Explanation: Refill, check and decrement form one invariant; a thread switch between the check and the decrement lets two callers spend the last token. The GIL does not make a multi line method atomic. A thread safe clock says nothing about the shared fields. Locking only refill still leaves the check then act race.

fields.Question: An LRU cache extends LinkedHashMap with accessOrder = true, and get is wrapped in a ReadWriteLock read lock for speed. Why is that wrong?
fields.Choices:
Read locks do not provide visibility in Java
LinkedHashMap cannot be used with locks
In access order mode get moves the entry to the tail, so it mutates the list and needs the write lock
get can throw because the map is ordered
fields.Correct: In access order mode get moves the entry to the tail, so it mutates the list and needs the write lock
fields.Explanation: With accessOrder true, LinkedHashMap.get relinks the accessed node, a structural change. Multiple readers doing that concurrently corrupt the list. Use a plain lock or a purpose built cache. ReadWriteLock read locks do give visibility. Locks work with any map, and ordering does not cause get to throw.
fields.Hint: In an LRU, a read is also a write.

fields.Question: A Go LRU cache protects its map and list with a sync.RWMutex and its Get method only takes RLock but calls list.MoveToFront. What happens under concurrent Gets?
fields.Choices:
Nothing, RLock allows any operation that does not touch the map
Readers block each other, so it is merely slow
A compile error because MoveToFront needs a pointer receiver
A data race on the list that -race reports, because MoveToFront writes shared pointers
fields.Correct: A data race on the list that -race reports, because MoveToFront writes shared pointers
fields.Explanation: Several goroutines can hold RLock at once, so concurrent MoveToFront calls write the same list pointers and corrupt it. Get must take Lock. RLock is only safe for genuinely read only work, whatever structure is touched. Readers do not block each other under RLock. The code compiles.
fields.Source:
Go sync package (https://pkg.go.dev/sync)
Go Data Race Detector (https://go.dev/doc/articles/race_detector)

fields.Choices:
cache.get(k), because ConcurrentHashMap reads are not thread safe
The return statement, which can return a stale reference
None, every call is on a concurrent map
The containsKey then put sequence, which can compute and store twice
fields.Correct: The containsKey then put sequence, which can compute and store twice
fields.Explanation: containsKey and put are separately atomic, so two threads can both miss and both compute, which is wasteful or wrong if compute has side effects. computeIfAbsent fixes it. ConcurrentHashMap reads are safe and the returned value is safely published. Thread safe calls do not make their composition atomic.

fields.Choices:
Make hits a buffered channel
Replace hits++ with atomic.AddInt64(&hits, 1) or guard it with a Mutex
Call runtime.Gosched() after hits++
Declare hits with var at package level
fields.Correct: Replace hits++ with atomic.AddInt64(&hits, 1) or guard it with a Mutex
fields.Explanation: hits++ is a read modify write and concurrent goroutines lose updates; the race detector reports it. An atomic add or mutex makes it a single synchronised step. Yielding only changes scheduling. Package level declaration does not add synchronisation. A channel could be used to funnel updates through one goroutine, but turning the int into a buffered channel as described is not a counter.
fields.Source:
Go Data Race Detector (https://go.dev/doc/articles/race_detector)
Go sync package (https://pkg.go.dev/sync)

fields.Question: An asyncio rate limiter does: if self.tokens > 0: await self.log_use(); self.tokens -= 1. Can two tasks overspend the last token?
fields.Choices:
No: asyncio is single threaded so nothing can interleave
Yes: the await between check and decrement lets another task pass the same check
No: the GIL prevents it
Yes, but only when uvloop is used
fields.Correct: Yes: the await between check and decrement lets another task pass the same check
fields.Explanation: Coroutines interleave at await points, and the await sits between the check and the update. Decrement before awaiting, or hold an asyncio.Lock across both. Single threading prevents preemption, not interleaving at awaits. The GIL is unrelated to cooperative scheduling. Any event loop behaves the same.
fields.Source:
Python Developing with asyncio (https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-dev.html)
Python asyncio Synchronization Primitives (https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-sync.html)

fields.Question: You need a per client rate limiter in Go: 10 requests per second with bursts of 20, shared by all request goroutines. Which choice is correct and simplest?
fields.Choices:
time.Tick(100 * time.Millisecond) per request handler
golang.org/x/time/rate.NewLimiter(10, 20), one per client in a mutex guarded map, calling Allow()
A plain int counter reset by a goroutine every second
A sync.WaitGroup with Add(20)
fields.Correct: golang.org/x/time/rate.NewLimiter(10, 20), one per client in a mutex guarded map, calling Allow()
fields.Explanation: rate.Limiter is a concurrency safe token bucket with rate and burst, and a mutex guarded map handles per client lookup. time.Tick per request creates a ticker per handler and does not share state across requests. A plain int races and a fixed window allows double bursts at boundaries. WaitGroup counts completions, not rate.
fields.Hint: There is a ready made token bucket.
fields.Source:
Go rate package (https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/time/rate)
Go sync package (https://pkg.go.dev/sync)
